draft.title: The Black Death arrives
card: The Black Death was a plague that reached Europe in 1347. It is thought to have come from Asia along trade routes, and it arrived by ship at ports in the Mediterranean.
The plague was spread by fleas that lived on rats. Fleas bit people and passed on the disease, and ships and towns full of rats helped it move.
It also spread from person to person, mainly when people lived close together in crowded towns.
Within a few years it killed about a third of Europe's people. Medieval people did not know about germs, so they could not explain or stop it.
draft.remember: The plague came along trade routes, spread by fleas and by people, and killed about a third of Europe.

a.q: How did the Black Death reach Europe in 1347?
opts: Along trade routes, carried by ships to ports
Through Crusader armies returning from Jerusalem
From poor harvests that spoiled food in towns
By peasants who left the countryside for cities
a.why: The plague travelled along trade routes and came by ship to Mediterranean ports. Peasants moving to cities is tempting, but that happened inside Europe and does not explain how the plague first arrived.
a.clue: Think about how goods and people travelled between Asia and Europe.

b.q: A town in medieval Italy has a port, many rats and crowded streets. Why was it likely to suffer badly from the plague in 1347?
opts: Rat fleas and close contact helped the disease spread
Its people had stopped trading with other places
Most of its people had already caught the disease
Its rats were killed, which left the fleas without hosts
b.why: Ships and rats brought fleas, and crowded streets let the disease pass from person to person. Stopping trade would have slowed the plague, not made it worse, because trade routes carried it.
b.clue: Look at what the port, the rats and the crowds each did.

a.best: Along trade routes, carried by ships to ports

b.best: Rat fleas and close contact helped the disease spread

problems.detail: The distractor 'Its rats were killed, which left the fleas without hosts' rests on a shaky premise. Historically, when rats died their fleas moved to human hosts, which helped spread plague to people. A student who knows this could be confused. A cleaner distractor would avoid the rat die-off idea.

check.summary: The facts, answers and explanations check out. One distractor in question b (rats killed, leaving fleas without hosts) could confuse students, because rat deaths actually drove fleas onto people.
